## Q1-(a)

```{r}
#| echo: true
read_and_merge <- function(){
  aux <- read_xpt("AUX_I.xpt")
  demo <- read_xpt("DEMO_I.xpt")
  merged <- inner_join(aux, demo, by = "SEQN")
  return(merged)
}

df_raw <- read_and_merge()
cat("Merged dataset dimensions (rows, columns):\n")
print(dim(df_raw))
```

I perform an inner join on the identifier `SEQN`. Only records that appear in both datasets are kept.We can now see the merged dimensions (4852,119)

## Q1-(b)

```{r}
clean_data <- function(df_raw){
  df_clean <- df_raw %>%
    mutate(
      # Gender: 1=Male, 2=Female
      gender = ifelse(RIAGENDR %in% c(99,999,-9,NA), NA, RIAGENDR),
      gender = factor(gender, levels = c(1,2), labels = c("Male","Female")),
      # Citizenship status
      citizenship = ifelse(DMDCITZN %in% c(99,999,-9,NA), NA, DMDCITZN),
      citizenship = factor(citizenship),
      # Income-to-poverty ratio (continuous)
      income_poverty = ifelse(INDFMPIR %in% c(99,999,-9,NA), NA, INDFMPIR),
      income_poverty = as.numeric(income_poverty),
      # Right ear tympanometric width
      tymp_right = ifelse(AUXTWIDR %in% c(99,999,-9,NA), NA, AUXTWIDR),
      tymp_right = as.numeric(tymp_right),
      # Left ear tympanometric width
      tymp_left = ifelse(AUXTWIDL %in% c(99,999,-9,NA), NA, AUXTWIDL),
      tymp_left = as.numeric(tymp_left)
    )
  return(df_clean)
}
df_clean <- clean_data(df_raw)
summary(df_clean %>% select(gender, citizenship, income_poverty, tymp_right, tymp_left))

```

I create a cleaned dataset starting from the merged data with 4582 observations.
All invalid/missing codes (-9, 99, 999) are recoded into R native `NA`.
`RIAGENDR` is converted to a labelled factor for gender.
`DMDCITZN` (citizenship status) is converted to a categorical factor.
`INDFMPIR` (income-to-poverty ratio) is kept as a continuous predictor.
`AUXTWIDR` and `AUXTWIDL` are the continuous tympanometric width outcomes for right and left ear, used in the Poisson regression models.

## Q1-(c)

```{r}
fit_poisson <- function(formula, data){
  mod <- glm(formula, family = poisson(link = "log"), data = data)
  irr_table <- tidy(mod, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) %>%
    select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) %>%
    rename(IRR = estimate, CI_low = conf.low, CI_high = conf.high, p_val = p.value)
  null_mod <- glm(update(formula, . ~ 1), family = poisson(link="log"), data = data)
  mcfadden_r2 <- 1 - as.numeric(logLik(mod)) / as.numeric(logLik(null_mod))
  fit_stats <- tibble(
    n = nrow(mod$model),
    AIC = AIC(mod),
    McFadden_pseudoR2 = mcfadden_r2
  )
  return(list(irr = irr_table, stats = fit_stats, model_obj = mod))
}
m1R <- fit_poisson(tymp_right ~ gender, df_clean)
m2R <- fit_poisson(tymp_right ~ gender + citizenship + income_poverty, df_clean)
m1L <- fit_poisson(tymp_left ~ gender, df_clean)
m2L <- fit_poisson(tymp_left ~ gender + citizenship + income_poverty, df_clean)
irr_all <- bind_rows(
  m1R$irr %>% mutate(Model = "1R: Right ~ Gender"),
  m2R$irr %>% mutate(Model = "2R: Right ~ Full"),
  m1L$irr %>% mutate(Model = "1L: Left ~ Gender"),
  m2L$irr %>% mutate(Model = "2L: Left ~ Full")
) %>%
  select(Model, term, IRR, CI_low, CI_high, p_val) %>%
  mutate(across(c(IRR, CI_low, CI_high), ~round(.x,3)), p_val = round(p_val,4))
stat_all <- bind_rows(
  m1R$stats %>% mutate(Model = "1R: Right ~ Gender"),
  m2R$stats %>% mutate(Model = "2R: Right ~ Full"),
  m1L$stats %>% mutate(Model = "1L: Left ~ Gender"),
  m2L$stats %>% mutate(Model = "2L: Left ~ Full")
) %>%
  select(Model, n, AIC, McFadden_pseudoR2) %>%
  mutate(across(c(AIC, McFadden_pseudoR2), ~round(.x,3)))
kable(irr_all, caption = "Incidence Risk Ratios from Poisson Regression Models", format = "html")
kable(stat_all, caption = "Model Fit Summary Statistics", format = "html")
```

Results are reported as incidence risk ratios (IRR). IRR \> 1 indicates a higher expected tympanometric width, and significance holds when the 95% CI does not contain 1.

In both simple and adjusted models, females have significantly greater tympanometric width than males. Citizenship category 2 is positively associated with wider width for both ears; citizenship category 7 is significant only for the right ear. Higher income-to-poverty ratio is linked to slightly smaller width.

The full adjusted models yield lower AIC and modest McFadden pseudo-\\(R\^2\\) (0.101 for right ear, 0.092 for left ear), showing citizenship and income improve model fit compared with gender-only models.

## Q1-(d)

This Poisson regression analysis examined associations between gender, citizenship, income-to-poverty ratio and tympanometric width. Females had significantly larger tympanometric width in both simple and fully adjusted models. Citizenship status and income-to-poverty ratio were also significant predictors. The full models had better fit than gender-only models. These findings suggest demographic and socioeconomic factors are associated with tympanometric width.
